Nothing here is verified yet. Every class below was proposed by clustering, which is exactly the step a previous study skipped when it published per-class numbers on a derived inventory. Treat this report as a look at what the pipeline produced, not as ground truth.

Whole pages, marks boxed

The defining property of this task is the ratio between the target and the page. Every mark the source annotates is boxed, coloured by kind. Exactly one box is red: the largest mark that carries a class identity, which is the one the caption measures — so the picture and its number always describe the same box. A crop gallery makes these look easy; this is what the matcher actually sees.

  • the largest labelled mark on that page — the one the caption measures
  • logo — queryable
  • signature — recorded, never queryable (a signature is a different mark every time it is made)
  • stamp — queryable

The Goods — every class, every instance

One row per class. What to look for: do all the crops in a row show the same mark? A row that mixes two marks is an over-merged cluster; two rows showing the same mark are a split that should be merged. Both are what the cluster and confusable audits exist to catch.

The Bads — what the haystack looks like

197,778 pages carry no labelled mark and serve as distractors: 26 from spods, 61 from staver, 469 from tobacco800, 197,222 from ucsf. These need no labels — only to be safe to score against, which the contamination rules decide.

  • logo — queryable

Near misses — the negatives that actually matter

A blank page is a trivial negative. The hard one is a real mark on a real scan that simply is not the mark being searched for. Each of these is a positive for one class and a negative for every other, which is why exhaustive verification turns a same-source page from a contamination risk into the most valuable negative available.

Scale — how big are these things?

The 2026-07-13 study measured a hard floor near 32px: below it no structural pipeline recovered anything, tiling and backends alike. A class built from sub-floor instances measures that floor rather than the method, which is why the builder refuses one by default.
